sections.h2: Which offices run property tax inside Morris County?
sections.html:
Three local offices share the work in Morris County, and none of them is the state. The Morris County Board of Taxation keeps the county records of taxable real estate, sets tax rates and equalization ratios, supervises the municipal tax assessors, reviews assessments and rules on appeals. Mail for the board goes to P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900.

The county has 39 municipalities, and each one runs its own assessor and tax office. New Jersey follows a strong home rule model, so the state neither writes local budgets nor receives any of the property tax money. A town's general rate comes from dividing the dollars it must raise by the total assessed value of its taxable property. Your bill is that rate multiplied by your own assessment (NJ Division of Taxation).

  • The municipal assessor values your Morris County house and answers questions about the number on your notice.
  • The Board of Taxation hears appeals of that number and publishes the rates for each town.
  • The Morris County Clerk records the deed when the house sells.

sections.h2: How pricey and how owner heavy are Morris County homes?
sections.html:
Morris County is a high value, mostly owner occupied county. The Census Bureau counts 524,251 residents in its July 2025 estimate, up from 509,285 at the 2020 census, spread over 460.97 square miles of land. Three quarters of households own, and the typical owned home is worth well over half a million dollars.

Owners with no mortgage still carry a monthly cost of $1,385, and much of that is the tax bill and insurance. When a Morris County owner falls behind, the unpaid tax is a real number that a buyer or closing attorney will want to see in writing.

sections.h2: What should a home seller know about the Morris County landscape?
sections.html:
Morris County sits about 30 miles west of New York City. Morristown is the seat, and the county has many commuter towns and no big city. Parsippany-Troy Hills is the most populous municipality at 56,162 residents in 2020, while Rockaway Township covers the most ground at 45.55 square miles. The county was created on March 15, 1739 from part of Hunterdon County and carries the name of Colonel Lewis Morris.

The land rises from the flatter Passaic River valley suburbs in the east to hills in the west. The high point is 1,395 feet in western Jefferson Township. The Rockaway, Whippany, Raritan and Black rivers drain different parts of the county, so a house in the lower east can sit in a very different setting than one on a western ridge. Ask your municipal office about any flood zone or steep slope issue before you list or accept an offer.

The county is divided into 39 municipalities, so an assessment and a tax rate in one town say little about the next town over. Compare your own notice with nearby sales before you decide whether an appeal or a quick sale makes more sense.

History shows up in the housing stock. Washington's army wintered at Jockey Hollow in 1779 and 1780, and Dover was a center of iron mining in the 1880s. Older homes in towns such as Morristown and Dover often need more repair work than newer subdivisions, which affects how a buyer prices an as-is sale.

sections.h2: How is a Morris County assessment set, and how do I appeal it?
sections.html:
You appeal to the Morris County Board of Taxation, and the petition must be received by April 1. Where a municipal revaluation or reassessment took place, the deadline moves to May 1. File Form A-1 with the comparable sales form, and remember that a postmark is not enough (NJ Division of Taxation).

All 21 New Jersey counties assess at 100 percent of true value, measured as of the October 1 assessment date. The Morris County board says an assessment is excessive only if it misses one of two standards. After a revaluation year, it must represent 100 percent of market value. In other years, it must fall inside the common level range, which is plus or minus 15 percent of the town's average ratio.

  • Use sales that closed before October 1, because later sales do not count as evidence.
  • Expect an in-person hearing, since the Morris County board has said it holds no virtual appeal hearings.
  • If the board rules against you, the Tax Court of New Jersey takes the next appeal, filed within 45 days of the board's judgment.
  • Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 may file straight with the Tax Court by the same April 1 or May 1 date.
  • An added or omitted assessment is appealed on Form AA-1, and the Tax Court is available directly when the aggregate exceeds $750,000.

sections.h2: Which property tax relief programs affect a Morris County sale?
sections.html:
Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ apply only to a principal residence, so a sale usually ends them for that house. Homeowners 65 or older can qualify for all three, and renters can qualify for ANCHOR only. The benefit follows the home you owned and occupied on October 1 of the application year. The state's 2026 application deadline was November 2, 2026, and it has passed (Division of Taxation FAQ).

The Division's home sale guide adds two timing rules. If you moved after October 1 of the application year, say so on the application or risk losing the benefit. A Senior Freeze participant who buys another New Jersey home waits two years, not the standard three, to set a new base year.

Local benefits also exist: a deduction for seniors and disabled persons, a veterans deduction, and an exemption for disabled veterans. The municipal tax office in your Morris County town handles those, so ask whether a deduction on the house you are selling ends at closing.

sections.h2: What happens at closing when a Morris County house sells?
sections.html:
The seller owes the state Realty Transfer Fee at recording, and every seller files a GIT/REP form with the deed. Resident sellers use form GIT/REP-3 to skip the estimated income tax payment, and any gain is reported later on the NJ-1040. The transfer fee schedule is on the Division's Realty Transfer Fee page.

The Morris County Clerk's Registry Department records deeds. It requires a cover sheet with every land document, a cover letter with the submitter's name and address, and a "Record & Return" or "Cancel & Return" note on the document itself. The Registry takes recordings between 8:00 AM and 4:00 PM and can be reached at 973-285-6130.

Ask the municipal tax office for the exact payoff on any unpaid quarter, and ask the closing attorney how the current year's tax will be split between buyer and seller. Those two figures decide how much of the Morris County sale price you keep.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Morris County property tax appeal?
faqs.a: File with the Morris County Board of Taxation, using Form A-1 and the comparable sales form. The board's mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900, and hearings take place in person.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for a Morris County tax appeal?
faqs.a: The petition must be received by April 1, or by May 1 where the municipality completed a revaluation or reassessment. The Division of Taxation treats the date as a receipt deadline, so mail early.

faqs.q: Does Morris County bill my property tax?
faqs.a: No, your municipality bills and collects it. The county board sets rates and equalization ratios and hears appeals, while your town's tax office issues the bill and supplies payoff figures at a sale.

faqs.q: Can I skip the county board if my house is assessed above $1,000,000?
faqs.a: Yes. An owner whose assessment is above $1,000,000 may file directly with the Tax Court of New Jersey, and the filing must still be received by April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer fee on a Morris County sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it, and it is collected at recording. A separate graduated percent fee also lands on the seller when the price tops $1,000,000.
